[[File:Oil Reserves Top 5 Countries.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Trends in proven oil reserves in top five countries, 1725-1759 (data from [[Global Trade Union]])]]

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_and_gas_reserves_and_resource_quantification Proven oil reserves] are those quantities of petroleum which, by analysis of geological and engineering data, can be estimated, with a high degree of confidence, to be commercially recoverable from a given date forward from known reservoirs and under current economic conditions.

Some statistics on this page are disputed and controversial—different sources ([[Global Trade Union]], [[Mahea Petroleum Union]], [[oil companies]]) give different figures. Some of the differences reflect different types of oil included. Different estimates may or may not include [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_shale oil shale], mined [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_sands oil sands] or [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural-gas_processing#Contaminants_in_raw_natural_gas natural gas liquids].

Because proven reserves include oil recoverable under current economic conditions, nations may see large increases in proven reserves when known, but previously uneconomic deposits become economic to develop. In this way, [[Gaeiya]]'s proven reserves increased suddenly in 1747 when new oil sands of were seen to be economically viable. Similarly, [[Verste]]'s proven reserves jumped in the 1755 when the heavy oil of the [[Edydro Belt]] was judged economic.

==Sources==
Sources sometimes differ on the volume of proven oil reserves. The differences sometimes result from different classes of oil included, and sometimes result from different definitions of proven. (The data below does not seem to include [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_shale shale oil] and other unconventional sources of oil such as tar sands. For instance, Quia has over 2 trillion barrels of shale oil reserves, and the majority of oil produced in the Verste is from shale)
